title: Why You Should Let Poorly Followed Routines Play Out s-play-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin advises against the common instinct to jump in and correct a sloppily executed routine as soon as it starts going wrong. He gives four reasons to instead observe from a distance and let it play out: it lets the teacher accurately diagnose whether the problem is behavior-based or a misunderstanding, it gives students the chance to catch and self-correct their own mistakes, it increases the odds students accept responsibility rather than becoming defensive, and it avoids adding stress or excitability that can spiral into a worse day. He is careful to note this doesn't mean allowing true chaos (like an unsafe hallway transition)—rather, the teacher observes, waits, and only then calmly asks for attention with a long pause before speaking. If the observation reveals genuine confusion about expectations, a full reteach is warranted instead.
points: Letting a sloppy routine play out lets the teacher accurately diagnose whether it's a behavior problem or a misunderstanding.
Watching without intervening gives students a chance to self-correct and recognize mistakes on their own.
Students who realize their own error are more likely to take responsibility than students corrected mid-routine.
Jumping in immediately adds stress and excitability that can escalate into a worse overall day.
This isn't total passivity—the teacher still steps in with a calm pause-and-attention cue and reteaches if genuine confusion, not defiance, caused the problem.
quotes: Upon noticing a class routine going off the rails, they immediately jump in to try and correct it.
It’s far better to take a step back and let the routine play out.
The only way to fix a sloppy routine so that it doesn’t happen again is to know precisely what went wrong.

When students know they’re being watched intently, especially by a teacher who faithfully holds them accountable for previously learned expectations, they develop the ability to recognize and correct their own mistakes.
When you jump in right away, on the other hand, they’re likely to become defensive, argumentative, and annoyed by your interruption.
Handling misbehavior with patience and composure, on the other hand, will calm and settle your students and refocus them on the task at hand.
Only then will your students begin looking inward at themselves and their responsibilities.
